articles.originalTitle: Thelma Golden To Step Down From Role as Director of Studio Museum in Harlem - ARTnews.com
articles.title: Thelma Golden to Step Down as Studio Museum in Harlem Director
articles.excerpt: Thelma Golden, director and chief curator of the Studio Museum in Harlem, announced she will step down from her position in late 2027, coinciding with her 20th anniversary.
articles.content: Thelma Golden, director and chief curator of the Studio Museum in Harlem, will step down from her position in late 2027, the museum announced. The announcement coincides with Golden's 20th anniversary in the role, which she assumed in 2006, and arrives one year after the museum reopened in a new building following a seven-year closure. The $125 million building was designed by architect David Adjaye and spans 82,000 square feet across seven floors. Kathryn C. Chenault, chair of the museum's board of trustees, stated that the board has formed a search committee to identify Golden's successor and retained an international executive search firm to assist. Golden will remain in her post until a replacement is hired. Before becoming director, Golden worked as a curatorial fellow at the museum and later held several positions at the Whitney Museum of American Art before returning to the Studio Museum in 2000 as deputy director. Credited with raising the profile of the museum through numerous exhibitions, Golden also received the Dorothy and Lillian Gish Prize in 2023.

articles.originalTitle: COP31 in Antalya: What the Climate Summit Means for Buildings and Cities - ArchDaily
articles.title: COP31 Climate Summit in Antalya Concludes with Initiatives for Buildings and Cities
articles.excerpt: The 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference in Antalya concluded with initiatives targeting building stock energy efficiency and urban resilience, while parties failed to reach consensus on the final overarching text amid debates over fossil fuels.
articles.content: Hosted by Türkiye with Australia leading negotiations, the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference concluded in Antalya on November 22, 2026, following extended talks. Bringing together nearly 200 parties alongside researchers and civil society, the summit addressed climate finance and adaptation, though participants failed to reach consensus on the proposed Antalya Pact due to disagreements over fossil fuels and finance. For the built environment, the Turkish Presidency introduced the Antalya Compact for Energy Efficient Buildings, a voluntary framework targeting a 25 percent reduction in global building operational energy intensity by 2035 compared to 2020 levels. During the ministerial meeting, 24 countries, the European Commission, and multiple stakeholders endorsed the compact. Meanwhile, the transition away from fossil fuels remained unresolved in the final political text, drawing objections from the European Union and the United Kingdom. Additionally, the Sustainable Urban Resilience Financing Facility, developed through Türkiye's İLBANK in partnership with UN-Habitat and the World Bank, was highlighted to help cities bridge the gap between climate commitments and investment-ready municipal projects.

articles.originalTitle: Mason & Fifth’s Belsize Park guesthouse was designed to be “domestic and low-impact” - Dezeen
articles.title: Belsize Park Guesthouse in London Redesigned with a Low-Impact Approach
articles.excerpt: Located in Ornan Court in London, the Mason & Fifth guesthouse has been redesigned through a collaboration between Holloway Li and New-works. The historic building features an interior focused on circular economy principles and natural materials.
articles.content: Opening its third site in London following Primrose Hill and Westbourne Park, the Mason & Fifth guesthouse occupies Ornan Court, a 19th-century mansion block in Belsize Park. Architecture practice New-works adapted the building for hospitality use, while design studio Holloway Li conceived the interiors. The design pursued a circular economy aesthetic aimed at being warm and low-impact. The ground level incorporates communal spaces including a shared kitchen, a lounge area with timber-frame chairs, and a snug painted in an ochre hue. Across the guesthouse's 56 apartments, bedrooms are furnished with demountable wardrobes fixed with metal brackets instead of fitted joinery. Kitchen countertops and splashbacks were crafted from limestone rejected by quarries due to inconsistencies. Almost all walls were rendered with multi-finish plaster, leaving surface imperfections visible. The project was shortlisted in the sustainable interior category of the Dezeen Awards.

articles.originalTitle: Efforts to save I.M. Pei’s Dallas City Hall likely headed to referendum - The Art Newspaper
articles.title: Efforts to Save I.M. Pei’s Dallas City Hall Likely Headed to Referendum
articles.excerpt: A grassroots campaign seeking to prevent the demolition of Dallas City Hall has gathered around 25,000 signatures, moving toward a public referendum vote in May 2027.
articles.content: The future of Dallas City Hall, designed by I.M. Pei and opened in 1978, has become the subject of a public dispute as local officials push to abandon and sell the structure. City leaders cite rising costs for necessary upgrades, which estimates place at $1.4bn over two decades. A campaign group supports demolishing the inverted pyramid building to create an entertainment district. In response, a grassroots coalition named Save Dallas City Hall gathered approximately 25,000 signatures to prompt a ballot referendum in May 2027. The coalition proposes a phased 10-year plan with estimated costs between $70m and $100m, arguing that the municipal government should continue operating from the facility. The modernist complex also features public sculptures by Henry Moore and Marta Pan. Preservation advocates note that maintaining the landmark is vital for recognising architectural and historical heritage.

articles.originalTitle: Momentous 61st Venice Biennale Ends With 2nd-Highest Visitor Turnout - Hyperallergic
articles.title: 61st Venice Biennale Concludes With High Visitor Turnout
articles.excerpt: Curated by the late Koyo Kouoh, the 61st Venice Biennale drew 714,015 visitors over its six-month run, marking the second-highest attendance in the event's history.
articles.content: The 61st Venice Biennale, curated by the late Koyo Kouoh, concluded on November 22 after a six-month run, reporting 714,015 visitors. Despite running three weeks shorter than previous editions to allow for the renovation of the Central Pavilion at the Giardini, the exhibition achieved the second-highest attendance in the event's history. The 2022 edition continues to hold the record with more than 800,000 visitors. Nearly 30,000 people attended the pre-opening events. Following Kouoh's death in May 2025, a team of collaborators comprising Rasha Salti, Marie Hélène Pereira, Gabe Beckhurst Feijoo, Siddhartha Mitter, and Rory Tsapayi carried out the exhibition. Featuring 109 international artists, many hailing from Africa and the Caribbean diasporas, the event included a record-high 100 participating countries. This high turnout follows peak visitor numbers at recent editions of the Venice Architecture Biennale and Venice International Film Festival, both organized under La Biennale di Venezia.

articles.originalTitle: inside ZHA’s royal theater in morocco, white curves meet crystalline caverns - Designboom
articles.title: Zaha Hadid Architects Completes Its First Realized Project in Africa
articles.excerpt: Designed by Zaha Hadid Architects, the Théâtre Royal de Rabat in Morocco is completed along the Bouregreg River. The building features a sweeping white exterior and an auditorium inspired by traditional motifs.
articles.content: Built in Rabat, Morocco, by Zaha Hadid Architects, the Théâtre Royal de Rabat marks the practice's first completed project in Africa. Situated along the Bouregreg River, the project was announced in 2010, with construction beginning in 2014. The building received a ceremonial inauguration in October 2024, followed by its first public performance in April 2026. Part of a cultural development program initiated by King Mohammed VI, the theater features an undulating profile inspired by the tidal landscape of the Bouregreg. The exterior utilizes molded glass-fiber-reinforced concrete panels supported by a system of structural ribs. The complex includes a 7,000-seat open-air amphitheater, a 1,821-seat main auditorium, and a 250-seat Studio Theatre. Developed with acoustic engineers at Arup New York, the main auditorium features angular, crystalline surfaces inspired by traditional Moroccan muqarnas. A vast, triple-height foyer inside connects public areas with interwoven staircases crossing different levels. Environmental systems on the site incorporate heat-recovery equipment, a thermal labyrinth, and a rainwater collection system for irrigation.

articles.originalTitle: Constantinople to Istanbul: One City, Two Empires – exhibition large print guide - Victoria and Albert Museum
articles.title: From Constantinople to Istanbul: Exhibition Explores Two Empires' History
articles.excerpt: The Victoria and Albert Museum released a large print guide for the Constantinople to Istanbul: One City, Two Empires exhibition, detailing the city's rich history, art, and architecture across Roman and Ottoman periods.
articles.content: In 324 CE, Roman emperor Constantine chose the ancient Greek city of Byzantion as a new capital, renaming it Nova Roma in 330 CE. The city soon became known as Constantinople, capital of the Byzantine Empire. Following the fall of the Byzantine capital in 1453, the city rose again as Istanbul, the new capital of the Ottoman Empire, remaining so until 1922. Located at the meeting point of Asia and Europe, the metropolis attracted merchants, artists, and pilgrims through its strategic sea routes. The exhibition examines the city's two distinct art and design traditions under Byzantine and Ottoman rule, featuring architecture, land walls, water-supply systems, and Christian relics. While Byzantine Constantinople featured central depictions of sacred figures in public spaces and churches, the Ottomans avoided such images, often utilizing calligraphy instead. Featuring objects from institutions such as the Istanbul Archaeological Museums and the Chester Beatty Library, the guide illuminates the multi-layered heritage of the historic metropolis.

articles.originalTitle: A Sprawling Exhibition of Latin American Art and Fashion Is Coming to NYC - Hyperallergic
articles.title: MoMA PS1 to Stage Exhibition Exploring Latin American Fashion and Visual Culture
articles.excerpt: Opening in April 2027, the Malvestir exhibition will feature twenty artists and designers examining the historical and contemporary dimensions of Latin American fashion.
articles.content: MoMA PS1 is preparing to open Malvestir in April 2027, an upcoming exhibition examining the visual lexicon of Latin American fashion. Curated by museum director Connie Butler and associate curator Elena Ketelsen González, the presentation features twenty creatives who interrogate Western appropriations of Indigenous crafts, textile waste, and the fetishization of regional styles. The lineup includes New York designers and textile artists reviving intergenerational weaving traditions, such as Willy Chavarria, Carla Fernández, Josh Tafoya, and David Ramirez Cotón. Several participants incorporate local artisan collaborations and street-style traditions to counter corporate reproduction and mainstream market co-optation. Arlene Dávila, a professor at New York University, notes that the current political climate and pressures for assimilation serve as a rallying call for visionaries rooted in their communities. The works on view draw directly from vernacular traditions, oral histories, and family memories, showcasing the full range and power of Latin American cultures against institutional marginalization.

articles.originalTitle: Russian strikes damage historic buildings in Kyiv and Odesa, including World Heritage sites - The Art Newspaper
articles.title: Russian Strikes Damage Historic Buildings in Kyiv and Odesa
articles.excerpt: Multiple cultural heritage sites in Ukraine, including UNESCO-listed locations in Kyiv and Odesa, sustained damage during recent Russian attacks.
articles.content: Russian strikes on November 19 and 20 damaged multiple heritage sites in Ukraine, including the UNESCO-listed St. Michael's Golden-Domed Cathedral and Monastery complex, the frescoed St. Volodymyr's Cathedral in Kyiv, and 12 cultural heritage sites in Odesa. Ukrainian Deputy Prime Minister Tetyana Berezhna reported that the Volodymyr Cathedral sustained damage to structural elements and paintings. Built in the 19th century, the neo-Byzantine cathedral features art by prominent historical painters. The adjacent Austrian embassy was also damaged in the attack. UNESCO issued a condemnation, noting that historic structures within Odesa's World Heritage property, including the 1834 Kalio Palace, suffered damage. The strikes occurred amid heightened tensions following attacks on the Kerch Bridge, statements by Russian leadership rejecting partial ceasefires, and remarks by US President Donald Trump regarding peace efforts. Meanwhile, several European countries are seeking to bar Russia from participating in the 2027 Architecture Biennale.

articles.originalTitle: angelo renna’s eight principles for welcoming non-human life back into our cities - Designboom
articles.title: Eight Principles for Welcoming Non-Human Life into Urban Design
articles.excerpt: Designer Angelo Renna has published an eight-principle guide for integrating non-human species into urban environments. The recommendations focus on allowing spontaneous green growth, reducing lawn maintenance, and incorporating natural habitats.
articles.content: As human activities over the past half-century have contributed to a significant decline in global wildlife populations, designer Angelo Renna has outlined an eight-principle framework for integrating non-human species into urban environments. The guidelines advocate for allowing urban ecosystems to emerge naturally without excessive landscaping control, alongside reducing the frequency of intensive lawn mowing, which research links to decreased plant and invertebrate diversity. Additional principles include incorporating decaying tree trunks and snags to provide food and shelter for various organisms, providing water sources beyond simple drinking facilities for amphibians and insects, and utilizing porous construction materials and dry-stacked bricks to form microhabitats. The framework also emphasizes choosing diverse multispecies vegetation communities over monocultures to increase ecological resilience against environmental stress. Ultimately, the proposals envision the future city not merely as a human-centric development process, but as a shared habitat characterized by interspecific co-evolution and coexistence between humans and other forms of life.

articles.originalTitle: About the Constantinople to Istanbul: One City, Two Empires exhibition - Victoria and Albert Museum
articles.title: Constantinople to Istanbul Exhibition Explores Sixteen Centuries of Art at V&A
articles.excerpt: The Victoria and Albert Museum presents Constantinople to Istanbul: One City, Two Empires, an exhibition featuring over 200 objects that explore 1,600 years of artistic production across the Byzantine and Ottoman empires.
articles.content: The Victoria and Albert Museum is hosting a comprehensive exhibition titled Constantinople to Istanbul: One City, Two Empires, which runs until 9 May 2027. The exhibition explores 1,600 years of artistic production spanning from AD 330 to 1922. It examines the enduring creative legacy of an imperial capital that shaped the Mediterranean world and beyond, highlighting the distinct yet connected traditions of both the Byzantine and Ottoman empires. The display showcases more than 200 objects across four main sections, featuring rare decorative arts, fine silks, ceramic tiles, mosaics, precious metalwork, jewellery, sculptures, manuscripts, and paintings. The exhibition is organized into four thematic sections: Roman Beginnings, Heaven and Earth, Power and Reach, and Life in the City. The opening section covers the refounding of the city in AD 330 as the capital of the Roman Empire, followed by sections exploring sacred imagery in Christianity, the visual spectacle of Ottoman court authority, and the cosmopolitan rhythms of urban life characterized by diverse languages and faiths. The exhibition concludes by tracing the influence of Byzantine and Ottoman art on 19th-century European culture.

articles.originalTitle: AOM Higher Education/Research: Utah State University Kem & Carolyn Gardner Learning & Leadership Building - Engineering News-Record
articles.title: Utah State University Kem and Carolyn Gardner Learning and Leadership Building Wins Award

articles.content: Located on the Logan campus of Utah State University, the Kem and Carolyn Gardner Learning and Leadership Building consolidates five academic centers from the Jon M. Huntsman School of Business under one roof. The 44,658-square-foot, three-story academic facility was designed by MHTN Architects, with Jacobsen Construction serving as the general contractor. Inspired by nearby Logan Canyon, the design team incorporated a hybrid steel and mass timber system, making it the university's first mass timber building. Exposed glulam columns and cross-laminated timber decking created a light-filled interior. The mass timber structure also supports the university's goal of achieving carbon neutrality by 2040. Reaching the project site required navigating through two active construction sites near Highway 89, demanding close coordination among all teams. During design development, structural, mechanical, and electrical systems were integrated into cavities to conceal conduits and ductwork while preserving the visual continuity of the timber.

articles.originalTitle: Building a Permanent Home for a Space Shuttle Was an Engineering Endeavor - Engineering News-Record
articles.title: New Exhibition Facility Opens for Space Shuttle Endeavor in Los Angeles
articles.excerpt: The Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center at the California Science Center has opened to exhibit the retired space shuttle Endeavor in the launch position. The $450 million project was built through specialized engineering.
articles.content: The $450 million Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center at the California Science Center has opened its doors. The facility houses the retired space shuttle Endeavor, which flew its final mission in June 2011, as the only shuttle globally exhibited in launch position. ZGF Architects, MATT Construction, and engineering teams designed a 200-foot-tall stainless-steel structure tailored to the shuttle stack geometry. Seismic analysis constituted the most challenging aspect of the project, requiring civil and aerospace engineers to account for potential earthquake impacts on the shuttle. The perimeter steel diagrid system was engineered to carry loads without internal columns. Six seismic isolator bearings separate the supporting concrete pad from the foundation, allowing independent movement during earthquakes. Strict safety measures were enforced throughout construction to protect the fragile thermal silica tiles covering the shuttle.

articles.originalTitle: Eight Dead, 18 Injured in Brooklyn Building Collapse Next to Construction Site - Engineering News-Record
articles.title: Eight Dead and 18 Injured in Brooklyn Building Collapse Near Construction Site
articles.excerpt: An adjoining 96-year-old three-story building collapsed into an excavation site in Brooklyn, New York, leaving 8 people dead and 18 injured. Authorities have launched multiple investigations into the incident.
articles.content: On November 11, a three-story building collapsed into an adjoining excavation site in the Brooklyn borough of New York, resulting in 8 fatalities and 18 injuries. Officials confirmed the dead included two children and two construction workers, while the Fire Department concluded rescue operations on November 12. City records list Townhouse Builders as the general contractor for the project at 2625 Bedford Ave. A project geotechnical report had warned that abutting structures required underpinning and that construction-related vibrations could adversely affect neighboring properties. A March 5 preconstruction survey documented visible cracking at 1321 Flatbush Ave., rating its north masonry facade as poor and its other facades as fair. Area residents reported feeling heavy impacts and shaking while construction was underway next door. Mayor Zohran Mamdani ordered safety inspections at approximately 100 other construction sites linked to companies involved in the project. New York Attorney General Letitia James stated that the Buildings Department would conduct a full investigation, alongside a separate probe launched by Brooklyn District Attorney Eric Gonzalez. The exact cause of the structural collapse remains undetermined pending the conclusion of ongoing investigations by municipal authorities.

articles.originalTitle: Biennale Arte 2026 | TAREK EL-ARISS | Emptying the Jars of War, or How We Learned to Love Nature - La Biennale di Venezia
articles.title: Tarek El-Ariss to Discuss War, Nature, and Water Politics at Biennale Arte 2026

articles.content: Tarek El-Ariss is scheduled to speak at an event during Biennale Arte 2026 on November 21, 2026. Taking place at Teatro Piccolo Arsenale from 16:00 to 17:30, the lecture will be introduced and moderated by Rasha Salti. The session addresses how crises and wars not only damage the environment but also unsettle perceptions of nature. Drawing from everyday scenes such as saving water jars for bathing during wartime in Lebanon, the discussion traces longer histories and mythologies of water and greenery from the Garden of Eden to Greek and Islamic traditions, while focusing on the oasis as a recurring fantasy. The lecture posits that environmental practices do not necessarily emerge from ethical choices, often arising instead through habit, fear, or the quest for survival. Sustainability is reframed as a negotiation that interrogates the politics of purity and control to imagine alternative futures. Admission to the event is free until venue capacity is reached.

articles.originalTitle: Biennale Arte 2026 | LERATO SHADI | Unfolding - La Biennale di Venezia
articles.title: Lerato Shadi's Performance Unfolding To Be Presented At Biennale Arte 2026
articles.excerpt: Lerato Shadi's performance titled Unfolding, focusing on memory and collective processes, will meet audiences on November 21, 2026, within Biennale Arte 2026.
articles.content: Shaped around memory, visibility, and collective processes, Unfolding is structured as a performance examining how meaning is produced and transmitted through bodies. The event will take place on November 21, 2026, from 12:00 to 12:40 in the Sala d’Armi E space. The work unfolds through a group relay structure where participants move to the stage, wrap a stone with red wool, and pass the transformed object to another participant. Through this repeated action, the object gradually changes form, accumulating time, touch, and traces of multiple hands. While wrapping becomes a gesture of protection and connection, passing the stone evokes histories and knowledge carried collectively rather than individually. Featuring Camille Badirou, Trovania Dellile, Viviana Medina, Rebecca Pokua Korang, and the artist herself, attendance requires a valid Biennale Arte 2026 admission ticket.

articles.originalTitle: Claude Monet | Waterlilies | L1406 - The National Gallery, London
articles.title: Claude Monet's 1905 Waterlilies Painting on Display in London
articles.excerpt: Claude Monet's 1905 painting Waterlilies forms part of his series inspired by his water gardens in Giverny. The artwork is housed at the National Gallery in London.
articles.content: After renting a house in Giverny west of Paris in 1883, Claude Monet eventually purchased the property and transformed the grounds into water gardens. Once the gardens matured, Monet turned to depicting them, making the water garden the subject of more than two hundred pictures. Between 1905 and 1908, he painted over sixty views of the pond exploring the contrast between tangible flowers and lily pads and the reflections of the unseen sky and overhanging trees. Housed at the National Gallery in London, Waterlilies exemplifies this series. In the painting, white flowers closest to the viewer feature purple accents for depth, while receding flowers are rendered in simple touches of white, yellow, pink, and red. The water itself consists of myriad tones of violets, blues, turquoise, and greens. The painting was included in Monet's 1909 exhibition at Durand-Ruel's gallery in Paris. Measuring 87 by 100 cm, the oil on canvas work is part of the Kenneth C. Griffin Collection.
